stem: Which expression gives the marginal utility of the nth unit of a commodity?
options: TUn − TUn−1
TUn ÷ n
TUn + TUn−1
TUn−1 − TUn
explanation: Correct option: (A). Marginal utility is the change in total utility from consuming one more unit, so MUn = TUn − TUn−1. TUn ÷ n is average utility, not marginal utility; adding the two totals has no meaning; and TUn−1 − TUn reverses the sign of the change.

stem: A consumer buys 5 units of commodity x when its price is Rs 40 per unit. Using cardinal utility analysis, under what condition will she buy a 6th unit?
options: At Rs 40 itself, since her total utility is still rising
Only if the price rises, as a higher price signals quality
Never, because her marginal utility is always zero there
Only if the price falls below Rs 40 per unit
explanation: Correct option: (D). By the law of diminishing marginal utility, the 6th unit is worth less to her than the 5th, so she will pay less for it; she buys it only when the price falls below Rs 40. This is why the demand curve slopes downward. Rising TU does not make the 6th unit worth Rs 40; a higher price lowers, not raises, demand; and nothing says MU is zero at the 6th unit.

stem: The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) of bananas for mangoes measures:
options: the mangoes the market requires in exchange for one more banana
the extra utility gained from one more banana
the mangoes given up for one more banana at constant utility
the extra income needed to buy one more banana
explanation: Correct option: (C). MRS = |ΔY/ΔX| is the amount of mangoes the consumer is willing to forego for an additional banana while keeping total utility unchanged. stem: Suppose two indifference curves IC1 and IC2 intersect at A (7 bananas, 10 mangoes). B (9, 7) lies on IC1 and C (9, 5) lies on IC2. Why does this situation lead to a contradiction?

B and C would then have to lie on one budget line

The vertical intercept falls and the line gets flatter
The horizontal intercept rises and the line gets steeper

stem: A consumer's income is Rs 120, the price of bananas is Rs 4 and the price of mangoes is Rs 6. Her income now rises by 50% and both prices double. How does her budget line change?
options: Shifts inward parallel; the slope stays −2/3
Shifts outward parallel; the slope stays −2/3
Pivots inward; the slope becomes −4/3
Does not change, as all values have risen
explanation: Correct option: (A). Old intercepts: 120/4 = 30 bananas and 120/6 = 20 mangoes. New income is Rs 180 and prices are Rs 8 and Rs 12, so new intercepts are 180/8 = 22.5 and 180/12 = 15. Both intercepts fall and the slope −8/12 = −2/3 is unchanged, so the line shifts inward in parallel. It would shift outward only if income rose faster than prices; it would be unchanged only if income also doubled; both prices rising in the same proportion cannot change the slope.

Reason (R): Bundles lying above the budget line are not affordable at the given prices and income.

stem: At a bundle on her budget line, a consumer's MRS of bananas for mangoes is 2, and bananas and mangoes have the same price. What should she do to raise her satisfaction?
options: Keep this bundle, since it is already the optimum
Buy fewer bananas and more mangoes than now
Cut spending on both goods by the same amount
Buy more bananas and fewer mangoes than now
explanation: Correct option: (D). She is willing to give up 2 mangoes for an extra banana, but the market asks only 1 mango (price ratio = 1). Buying one more banana by giving up one mango leaves her with more than she needed, so she moves to a preferred bundle. MRS (2) ≠ price ratio (1), so this is not the optimum; moving the other way lowers satisfaction; spending less than her income is never optimal with monotonic preferences.

stem: A consumer is on her budget line where her MRS of bananas for mangoes is 1. The price of bananas is Rs 4 and the price of mangoes is Rs 2. How should a rational consumer adjust?
options: Buy fewer bananas and more mangoes
Buy more bananas and fewer mangoes
Stay put, since her MRS is below 2
Spend less than her income and save
explanation: Correct option: (A). The price ratio is p1/p2 = 4/2 = 2: giving up one banana frees Rs 4, which buys 2 mangoes. She needs only 1 mango to stay as well off (MRS = 1), so giving up bananas for mangoes makes her better off. She keeps doing so until MRS rises to equal 2. Buying more bananas moves her away from the optimum; MRS < price ratio is not an equilibrium; and with monotonic preferences unspent income is wasted.

stem:
Assertion (A): A fall in the price of a normal good raises the quantity of it demanded.
Reason (R): For a normal good, both the substitution effect and the income effect of a price fall increase its demand.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

explanation: Correct option: (A). When the price falls, the consumer substitutes towards the now-cheaper good (substitution effect), and her purchasing power rises, which raises demand for a normal good (income effect). stem: The price of a good falls. For this consumer the income effect reduces the demand for the good and is stronger than the substitution effect. What can be concluded?
options: It is a normal good and its demand rises
It is a Giffen good and its demand falls
It is an inferior good and its demand still rises
It is a substitute good and its demand is unchanged
explanation: Correct option: (B). An income effect that lowers demand when purchasing power rises means the good is inferior; if this effect outweighs the substitution effect, demand falls with the price, i.e. demand is positively related to price: a Giffen good. For a normal good both effects raise demand; demand would still rise only if the substitution effect were stronger; 'substitute' describes a relation between two goods, not this case.

explanation: Correct option: (B). Expenditure stays the same only when the percentage rise in quantity equals the percentage fall in price, i.e. eD = 1. With elastic demand expenditure would rise; with inelastic demand it would fall; with perfectly inelastic demand it would fall by the full 10%.

stem: Based on the case, what happened to consumers' total expenditure on the fresh lime soda after the price increase, and why?
options: It rose to Rs 8,096, as demand is price inelastic
It fell to Rs 7,360, as demand is price elastic
It stayed at Rs 8,000, as demand is unit elastic
It fell to Rs 7,904, as demand is price inelastic
explanation: Correct option: (A). Expenditure before = 40 × 200 = Rs 8,000; after = 44 × 184 = Rs 8,096. Price rose 10% while quantity fell only 8%, so eD = 0.8 < 1 (inelastic) and expenditure moves in the same direction as price. Rs 7,360 (40 × 184) uses the old price; Rs 7,904 is not P × Q at either price; unit elasticity would require an exact 10% fall in sales.

stem:
Assertion (A): The demand for luxury goods is generally price inelastic.
Reason (R): The demand for a good is likely to be elastic when close substitutes for it are easily available.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (D). A is false: demand for luxuries is very responsive to price changes and is generally elastic (eD > 1); it is necessities whose demand is inelastic. R is true: easy availability of close substitutes makes demand elastic.

stem: Based on the case, if the stall owner cuts the price of a mango shake from Rs 60 to Rs 50, what will happen to consumers' daily expenditure on mango shakes?
options: It will rise, because more glasses will be sold
It will fall, because each glass earns Rs 10 less
It will rise by Rs 10 times the number of extra glasses sold
It will stay at Rs 6,000, as elasticity is 1 throughout
explanation: Correct option: (D). Demand pq = 6,000 is a rectangular hyperbola, so price × quantity is always Rs 6,000 and |eD| = 1 at every point. At Rs 60, q = 100; at Rs 50, q = 120; expenditure is 6,000 both times. More glasses are sold, but the 20% rise in quantity exactly offsets the lower price, so expenditure neither rises nor falls.
